Cancer “survival rates” in the U.S. are usually reported as 5-year *relative* survival (how likely someone is to live at least five years after diagnosis compared with similar people without that cancer). They vary enormously by cancer type and—most importantly—by stage at diagnosis; some cancers have high overall survival while others remain difficult to treat, especially when found late.

- Chordoma (~300–350 cases/year in the U.S.)
- Adrenocortical carcinoma (~200–700 cases/year in the U.S.; often cited as ~0.5–2 per million/year)
- Uveal (ocular) melanoma (~2,000 cases/year in the U.S.)
- Merkel cell carcinoma (~3,000 cases/year in the U.S.)
- Malignant mesothelioma (~3,000 cases/year in the U.S.)

- Esophageal cancer (21.9%)
- Liver & intrahepatic bile duct cancer (22.0%)
- Lung & bronchus cancer (28.1%)
- Acute myeloid leukemia (32.9%)
- Stomach (gastric) cancer (37.9%)
